title: Collections: Maps, Sets, Queues and Heaps
intro: `std::collections` has what lies beyond `Vec`: a hash map, a sorted map, sets, a double-ended queue, a priority queue and a linked list. All of them ship with the standard library, and the docs say `Vec` and `HashMap` are the right starting point.

coming_from.go: Go gives you a map and a slice, and `container/heap` for a priority queue. Rust adds `BTreeMap` (keys kept sorted), `HashSet`, `VecDeque` (a queue) and `BinaryHeap`, which pops the largest first, so wrap items in `Reverse` for smallest first.
coming_from.kotlin: `BTreeMap` is `sortedMapOf` (a `java.util.TreeMap` on the JVM), `VecDeque` is Kotlin's own `ArrayDeque`, and `HashSet` is `hashSetOf`, not `setOf`, which remembers insertion order. The catch is `BinaryHeap`, which pops the largest first where `java.util.PriorityQueue` pops the smallest, so wrap items in `Reverse`.
coming_from.python: `HashSet` is `set`, `VecDeque` is `deque`, and `BinaryHeap` replaces `heapq`, but it pops the largest first, so wrap items in `Reverse`. `BTreeMap` keeps keys sorted, which no Python built-in does.
coming_from.typescript: `HashMap` and `HashSet` are like `Map` and `Set`, but a Rust `HashMap` does not remember insertion order. `VecDeque` is a queue you can add to and remove from at both ends, and `BinaryHeap` and `BTreeMap` have no built-in JavaScript equivalent.
coming_from.java: `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `HashSet`, `VecDeque` and `BinaryHeap` map to `HashMap`, `TreeMap`, `HashSet`, `ArrayDeque` and `PriorityQueue`. Watch the heap: `PriorityQueue` gives the smallest first, `BinaryHeap` gives the largest, so wrap items in `Reverse` to flip it.
coming_from.csharp: `Dictionary`, `SortedDictionary`, `HashSet`, `Queue<T>` and `PriorityQueue` are close to `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `HashSet`, `VecDeque` and `BinaryHeap`. `Queue<T>` only adds at the back, where `VecDeque` adds at both ends. `BinaryHeap` pops the largest first, the opposite of C#'s `PriorityQueue`. And `map[key] += 1` doesn't compile on a Rust map: use `entry(key).or_insert(0)`.
coming_from.c: The C standard library has `qsort` and `bsearch` but no map, set, deque or heap, so you'd use sorted arrays and hand-rolled lookups. Rust ships a hash map, a sorted map, sets, a deque and a heap, all generic and freeing their own memory.
coming_from.cpp: `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `HashSet`, `VecDeque` and `BinaryHeap` correspond to `unordered_map`, `map`, `unordered_set`, `deque` and `priority_queue`, and `priority_queue` is a max-heap too. `counts[w] += 1` doesn't compile, because Rust's `[]` never inserts; use `entry(w).or_insert(0)`.

notes: Which one? `Vec` for a list, `HashMap`/`HashSet` for lookups, `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` when you need keys in order or ranges like `map.range(10..20)`, `VecDeque` for a queue, `BinaryHeap` for "give me the biggest next".

The std docs call a `HashMap`'s order "arbitrary", and the default hasher (the code that turns a key into a number) is randomly seeded, so the order can differ between runs. If the output has to be stable, sort it or use a `BTreeMap`.

`text.split_whitespace().collect()` builds a `HashSet` because of the type you wrote on the left: `collect()` can build any collection, and the annotation picks which. The set holds `&str` views into `text`, so no word is copied. That works because `text` lives longer than `seen`, and the compiler checks that for you.

`VecDeque` is a ring buffer. The docs give adding or removing at either end a cost of O(1) (amortized for adding: averaged over the occasional resize). Removing the first item of a `Vec` is O(n): every other item shifts down.
`Reverse(n)` is a tiny wrapper that flips the comparison, so the max-heap hands out the smallest `n` first. The heap itself is unchanged.

gotcha.title: Bumping a counter with map[key] += 1
gotcha.looks_fine: `counts[w]++` is the most normal line in Go. The key is even there already, since we inserted "cat" first.
gotcha.rust_sees: `counts[w]` is read-only in Rust. A `HashMap` implements `Index` (read with `[]`) but not `IndexMut`, so you cannot assign through it, whether or not the key exists.
gotcha.why: This is a rule of the library, not a safety proof. A write through `[]` would have to either panic on a missing key or insert one, and `HashMap` chose to offer no write through `[]` at all. Writes go through methods that say what happens: `entry(w).or_insert(0)` (insert if missing), `get_mut(w)` (an `Option`, so you handle missing), or `insert`.

go.says: Go runs this and prints map[cat:2]. `counts[w] += 1` works for any key, because a missing one starts at 0.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too, for a different reason: `counts[w]` is an `Int?` (the key might be missing), so `counts[w] += 1` doesn't compile. You write `counts[w] = (counts[w] ?: 0) + 1` or use `merge`.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:5:19: error: operator call is prohibited on a nullable receiver of type 'Int?'. Use '?.'-qualified call instead.
        counts[w] += 1
                  ^^

python.says: Python prints {'cat': 2}. `counts[w] += 1` works because the key is already there. With a missing key it would raise KeyError, which is why counting code usually reaches for `Counter` or `defaultdict(int)`.

typescript.says: Prints { cat: 2 }. On a plain object `counts[w] += 1` compiles and works when the key exists. A missing key would quietly give `NaN`, since `undefined + 1` is `NaN`.

java.says: Java's Map has no `[]`, so the natural line is `counts.put(w, counts.get(w) + 1)`, and it prints {cat=2}. If the key were missing, `get` would return null and the `+ 1` would throw a NullPointerException.

csharp.says: The Dictionary indexer supports `+=`, so this prints [cat, 2]. Because the key is already there it works; with a missing key it would throw a KeyNotFoundException.

c.says: C has no map type and no operator overloading, so `counts[w]` can't take a string key; you call your own lookup function, as in the lesson.

cpp.says: `counts[w] += 1` works on `std::map` and prints `cat: 2`. Be aware that `[]` quietly inserts a 0 for any missing key, even when you only meant to read it.

kotlin.code:
import java.util.PriorityQueue

fun main() {
    val text = "the cat saw the dog and the cat ran"

    val counts = text.split(" ").groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
    val top = counts.entries
        .sortedWith(compareBy({ -it.value }, { it.key }))
        .take(3)
        .map { it.key to it.value }
    println("top: $top")

    val byName = sortedMapOf("zoe" to 31, "ana" to 30, "mia" to 28)
    println("sorted: $byName")

    val seen = text.split(" ").toSet()
    println("${seen.size} unique words, has dog: ${"dog" in seen}")

    val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf("a", "b"))
    queue.addLast("c")
    val first = queue.removeFirst()
    println("served $first, waiting $queue")

    val heap = PriorityQueue(listOf(5, 1, 8, 3))
    print("smallest first:")
    while (heap.isNotEmpty()) print(" ${heap.poll()}")
    println()
}

python.code:
import heapq
from collections import Counter, deque

text = "the cat saw the dog and the cat ran"

# Counter: count words, then sort by count and then by word
counts = Counter(text.split())
top = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))[:3]
print(f"top: {top}")

# no sorted dict in std: dicts keep insertion order, so sort the items
by_name = {"zoe": 31, "ana": 30, "mia": 28}
print(f"sorted: {dict(sorted(by_name.items()))}")

# set: unique items, fast "is it in there?"
seen = set(text.split())
print(f"{len(seen)} unique words, has dog: {'dog' in seen}")

# deque: a queue. Append at the back, pop at the front, both cheap.
queue = deque(["a", "b"])
queue.append("c")
first = queue.popleft()
print(f"served {first!r}, waiting {list(queue)}")

# heapq turns a plain list into a heap that pops the smallest first
heap: list[int] = []
for n in [5, 1, 8, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(heap, n)
print("smallest first:", end="")
while heap:
    print(f" {heapq.heappop(heap)}", end="")
print()

queues.kt.code:
import java.util.PriorityQueue
import java.util.TreeMap

fun main() {
    val q = ArrayDeque<String>()
    q.addLast("b")
    q.addFirst("a")
    println("ArrayDeque: $q, class: ${q.javaClass.name}")
    println("removeFirst: ${q.removeFirst()}")

    val log = sortedMapOf(10 to "boot", 25 to "login", 40 to "upload")
    println("sortedMapOf: $log, runtime class: ${log.javaClass.name}")
    // The static type of `log` is SortedMap, which has no floorKey: build a TreeMap for that.
    val tree = TreeMap(log)
    println("TreeMap floorKey(30): ${tree.floorKey(30)}, ceilingKey(30): ${tree.ceilingKey(30)}")

    println("setOf is a ${setOf(3, 1, 2).javaClass.name}")
    println("mutableMapOf is a ${mutableMapOf(3 to 1).javaClass.name}")
    println("hashSetOf is a ${hashSetOf(3, 1, 2).javaClass.name}")

    val a = setOf(1, 2, 3, 4)
    val b = setOf(3, 4, 5)
    println("a intersect b: ${a intersect b}, a is still: $a")

    val pq = PriorityQueue(listOf(3, 9, 4, 1))
    println("PriorityQueue peek: ${pq.peek()}")
}
